newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli official quits over Netanyahu "screw-ups".
newsitem.headline: Israeli official quits over Netanyahu "screw-ups".

text.p: Israel's deputy finance minister resigned on Tuesday, saying a main reason was Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's "major screw-ups and mistakes".

David Magen said in his first radio interview after handing in his resignation letter that the prime minister had agreed to give up $50 million in U.S. aid in secret talks with Jordan's King Hussein on May 8.
Magen told Israel Radio the resignation allowed him to speak freely on matters that troubled him.

"If I, for example, see that the prime minister has given up $50 million of the civilian aid in order to transfer it to the Jordanian kingdom...and opposite that the finance ministry has to sit and try to convince government ministries to cut another 700 million shekels...today I can go to the parliament and say that that is a stupid move and it must be stopped."
Magen said Netanyahu made the pledge to King Hussein at secret talks at Aqaba, Jordan, on May 8. Netanyahu's spokesmen were not immediately available for comment.

"I mentioned three weeks ago that certain expressions by the prime minister in addition to all sorts of major screw-ups and mistakes caused me to think that I can contribute more in the parliament than as part of the executive," Magen said.
Magen, of Netanyahu's Likud-Gesher-Tsomet parliamentary faction, first threatened to resign three weeks ago.

At the time he said Netanyahu's response to a prosecutors' decision in April not to charge him in a government scandal was the last straw. Magen at the time said Netanyahu had insulted Israelis' intelligence and called for early elections.
Netanyahu insisted the prosecutors' decision vindicated him in the affair over the short-lived appointment of an attorney general in January.
Magen's resignation was the latest in a string of embarrassments Netanyahu has suffered over appointees.

Among them, on May 13, Israel's new ambassador to Jordan, Oded Eran, resigned over not being informed of the Aqaba meeting. Netanyahu's first justice minister stepped down last August to stand trial for influencing a witness. He was acquitted last week.
